newsitem.title: USA: Odwalla sees extended sales decline.
newsitem.headline: Odwalla sees extended sales decline.

text.p: Odwalla Inc chief executive Stephen Williamson said the company's sales decline "will be substantial for some period of time" as a result of the incidents in which the E.coli bacteria infected some drinkers of Odwalla juice.
However, Williamson said the decline will not be as sharp as 50 percent, which is the amount of product Odwalla has eliminated from its line because of the apple juice scare.
Odwalla executives said a U.S. Food and Drug Administration report confirmed company findings that E.Coli was not present at Odwalla's processing plants.
The FDA's findings, completed last week, confirmed "this is not just an Odwalla problem but an issue for the entire industry," Williamson said.

The issue is that a particular strain of E.coli, referred to as O157:H7, is resistant to traditional fruit washing, safe processing and testing practices of the fresh juice industry. Williamson said Odwalla will not be making apple juice for the forseeable future until Odwalla, working with the industry and government, finds a way to eradicate that E.coli strain from apple juice.
He and other Odwalla officers said it will take time to study possible eradication methods but the answer will likely be some kind of application of heat, or pasteurization.

Odwalla became linked to an outbreak of E.coli in October in which several young children became seriously ill and about 50 people in all sickened with the E.coli bacteria, many of them after drinking Odwalla apple juice.
One child died earlier this month from complications said to result from drinking Odwalla juice.

The Dinuba, Calif.-juice-maker, which built a business on producing wholesome natural juices, recalled 16 of its products immediately after the first E. coli cases were reported, removing them from 4,600 stores in its distribution region.
The FDA and the company have been investigating since.
Friday, the FDA completed its field investigation, finding no E.coli O157:H7 in Odwalla's processing plant or facilities.

Odwalla executives and some microbiology advisors, gathered today to respond to press questions about the FDA report and its own plans, said the problem appears to be not isolated to Odwalla but one that affects the fresh apple juice industry generally. By fresh, the group said they mean producers of juices without preservatives or pasteurization.
"No E.coli whatsoever has been found in our plant or facilities," Williamson said.

But advising microbiologists Dr. Michael Doye of the University of Georgia and Dr Nick Nickelson of Red Mesa Microbiology food safety consulting firm, said the strain of E.coli linked to the recent outbreak is resistant to the acids in apple juice and which kill other types of E.coli.

With this current strain "We are rewriting the rule book of microbiology," said Doyle, adding that current industry washing, processing and testing procedures are apparently not enough to catch this strain.
Accordingly, they and Odwalla said they are recommending that the whole fresh apple juice industry halt production.
The two doctors said there is no evidence to suggest other types of fresh fruit juices are susceptible to the E.coli O157:H7 strain, although they did not say why.
They also said that fresh apples themselves should not be suspect if they are carefully washed.
"It is on the surface," Doyle said.
The only theory the internal investigation has as yet as to how Odwalla apple juice got contaminated with the E.coli strain is through deers coming into the orchards to eat the apples, he said.
